lessons.title: Prohibited practices (Article 5)
lessons.subtitle: Eight AI practices that have not been allowed to exist in the EU since 2 February 2025
keyConcepts: Fine of up to 7% of annual turnover

sections.title: The risk-based approach and the off switch
sections.content:
The AI Act bans very little. Eight practices, listed in **Article 5**, the unacceptable-risk level. Below it Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 stacks high risk (Article 6 in conjunction with Annexes I and III), limited risk with a transparency duty (Article 50), and the remainder at minimal risk. Four levels.

Article 5 is the only level without a compliance path. Either the system is one of the eight prohibited patterns, and then it goes. Or it is not. The prohibitions have applied since **2 February 2025** (Article 113, point (a)). No transition period, no SME exemption.

Prohibited means what it says. Not placed on the market, not put into service, not used (Article 5(1)). The penalty frame is the harshest in the whole Regulation: **up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover** (Article 99(3)), whichever figure is higher.

The authoritative reading of Article 5 is the Commission's **Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices** of 4 February 2025. They work through each of the eight categories in points (a) to (h) with concrete case groups.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 5 knows no middle way. Eight practices have been prohibited since 2 February 2025, under the harshest fine frame in the Regulation: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of annual turnover (Article 99(3)).

sections.title: The eight prohibited practices in Article 5(1), points (a) to (h)
sections.content:
Article 5(1) lists eight categories, and every one of them hits a real use case:

- **Point (a):** manipulative or subliminal techniques that cause significant harm. A dark-pattern bot that talks consumers into insurance.
- **Point (b):** exploiting vulnerability arising from age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation. AI marketing that targets people in debt with credit offers.
- **Point (c):** social scoring with detrimental treatment in an unrelated context. A supplier score that couples the managing directors' social-media activity to payment terms.
- **Point (d):** predictive policing based solely on profiling.
- **Point (e):** untargeted scraping of facial images to build databases, the Clearview AI prohibition.
- **Point (f):** emotion recognition in the workplace and in education institutions. The exception covers medical or safety reasons only. Software that reads facial expressions in interview videos has been prohibited since February 2025.
- **Point (g):** biometric categorisation by race, political opinion, religion, trade-union membership, or sex life.
- **Point (h):** real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces. Narrowly drawn exceptions for law enforcement only (Article 5(2) to (7), Annex II).
sections.keyTakeaway: The eight categories in points (a) to (h) are exhaustive. Emotion recognition at work (point (f)) and biometric categorisation (point (g)) hit SMEs most often.

sections.title: What an SME really has to examine
sections.content:
The rule of thumb: **if a tool measures emotions, biometrics, or social behaviour and attaches consequences to the result, it needs checking against Article 5.**

Typical cases from the working week.

- A plastics manufacturer wants to spot stress in machine operators by webcam and optimise shifts. Prohibited under point (f).
- Recruitment vendors are still advertising personality analysis from interview videos in 2026. A textbook point (f) infringement.
- An insurer scores applicants on public social-media posts. Prohibited under point (c), as soon as the detrimental treatment is unrelated to the context.

The check. Go through every piece of software with one question. Does it measure emotions, biometrics, or social behaviour, or does it steer decisions? Allow 30 to 60 minutes per system.

Free initial information has come from the Federal Network Agency's AI Service Desk since July 2025. Consent from the person affected, or approval from the works council, does not cure an Article 5 infringement. The prohibition holds regardless.

**Your next step:** if a tool like that turns up in your organisation, stop the use and get legal advice. Article 5 infringements cost up to EUR 35 million or 7% of turnover.
sections.keyTakeaway: A simple check, 60 minutes per tool. Consent cures nothing: Article 5 is an outright prohibition, not a consent-based legal basis.

quiz.questionText: A plastics manufacturer with 120 employees wants to use webcams to detect whether machine operators are stressed and optimise shifts. Is this permitted?

answerOptions.text: Yes, because it is used only for shift planning
Yes, with the employees' and works council's consent
No. Article 5(1), point (f), prohibits emotion recognition in the workplace
Yes, provided the data is processed only internally

quiz.explanation: Article 5(1), point (f), prohibits emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions. Consent, or a works council, does not cure the infringement. The only exception covers medical or safety purposes, such as fatigue detection in professional drivers.

quiz.questionText: What is the maximum fine for an infringement of Article 5?

answerOptions.text: Up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% of annual turnover
Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of annual turnover
Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover
Up to EUR 50 million or 10% of annual turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 99(3) sets the highest level of administrative fines for infringements of Article 5: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. The level for infringements listed in Article 99(4) is one step lower at EUR 15 million or 3%.

quiz.questionText: An insurer scores applicants using public social-media posts and treats them less favourably in a way unrelated to the insurance context. Which practice is this?

answerOptions.text: A high-risk system under Annex III, point 5
Prohibited social scoring under Article 5(1), point (c)
Limited risk with a transparency obligation under Article 50
Minimal risk because the social-media data is public

quiz.explanation: Article 5(1), point (c), prohibits assessments based on social behaviour where they lead to detrimental treatment in an unrelated context. Using social-media data in insurance pricing is the standard example of such a context mismatch. The public availability of the data does not alter the classification.

lessons.title: High risk: Annex I and Annex III
lessons.subtitle: Two routes into the high-risk class, eight use areas, and one exception you have to document

sections.title: Route 1: a safety component of a regulated product under Article 6(1)
sections.content:
AI in a lift control is high-risk. Not because of Annex III, but because the first route into the high-risk class runs through **Annex I**. There the Regulation lists around 20 EU harmonisation acts. Machinery Regulation 2023/1230, Medical Devices Regulation 2017/745, IVDR 2017/746, Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC, Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, Lifts Directive 2014/33/EU, motor-vehicle type approval, aviation under EASA, rail, and marine equipment.

The test in **Article 6(1)** has two steps. An AI system is high-risk where it is either the safety component of an Annex I product or is itself such a product, **and** the sectoral legislation requires a third-party conformity assessment.

Examples from the SME world.

- A machinery builder puts an AI module into a plant control with a protective shutdown. Safety component under the Machinery Regulation, therefore high-risk.
- AI in a lift control under Lifts Directive 2014/33/EU.
- A medical AI device under the Medical Devices Regulation.

Legal consequence: the sectoral conformity assessment applies **together with** the AI Act obligations in Articles 8 to 15.
sections.keyTakeaway: Build AI into an Annex I product and it is high-risk once the Article 6(1) conditions are met, the third-party conformity assessment included. The assessment runs through the sectoral act plus Articles 8 to 15 of the AI Act.

sections.title: Route 2: stand-alone high-risk systems under Article 6(2) and the eight Annex III areas
sections.content:
**Article 6(2)** is the second route, independent of the first. An AI system is high-risk where it is used in one of the **eight Annex III areas**. Paragraphs 1 and 2 stand side by side, and paragraph 3 holds a narrow counter-exception for pure support functions:

1. **Biometrics:** remote biometric identification, categorisation by sensitive attributes, emotion recognition where Article 5 does not prohibit it outright.
2. **Critical infrastructure:** AI as a safety component in the operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, water, gas, heating, electricity. The SME case: municipal utilities and regional energy suppliers.
3. **Education and vocational training:** admission and assessment AI, examination monitoring. Training firms with e-learning, vocational schools with examination software.
4. **Employment and HR:** recruitment, **CV screening**, and candidate evaluation (point 4(a)), plus work relationships, promotion, termination, task allocation, performance monitoring (point 4(b)). CV ranking in an applicant-tracking system can fall under point 4(a). The concrete intended purpose still has to be examined.
5. **Essential services:** eligibility for public assistance, creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing, emergency-call prioritisation. The SME case: insurance brokers, financial-service providers.
6. **Law enforcement** and 7. **migration, asylum, border control:** public-authority territory, rarely relevant to an SME.
8. **Administration of justice and democratic processes:** assistants for interpreting law (Annex III, point 8(a)), AI intended to influence elections (point 8(b)). The SME case: legal tech in law firms.

Providers meet Article 16 together with Articles 9 to 15. Risk management, data quality under Article 10, technical documentation under Article 11, logging under Article 12, transparency under Article 13, human oversight under Article 14, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity under Article 15. Deployers meet Article 26. The fundamental rights impact assessment in Article 27 binds only the addressees named there, not every private deployer of a high-risk system. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets **2 December 2027** for stand-alone Annex III systems and **2 August 2028** for product-embedded high-risk systems.
sections.keyTakeaway: Annex III names eight areas with concrete sub-cases. HR ranking can fall under point 4. The high-risk dates in 2027 and 2028 have been law since 27 July 2026, and the Article 27 impact assessment binds only the addressees named there.

sections.title: The exception in Article 6(3)
sections.content:
**Article 6(3)** lets a system used in an Annex III area fall outside the high-risk class where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making. The exception can apply where the AI system:

- **(a)** performs a narrow procedural task;
- **(b)** only improves the result of a human activity already completed;
- **(c)** detects decision patterns or deviations from earlier patterns without replacing or influencing the completed human assessment without proper human review; or
- **(d)** performs a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case.

**Profiling rules the exception out.** Whoever relies on Article 6(3) documents the self-assessment under Article 6(4) and registers the system in the EU database under Article 49(2).

In practice: an applicant-tracking vendor might take its pre-sorting module out of the high-risk class through Article 6(3). Whether that classification holds is something the **deployer** checks independently. Trust the provider blindly and you answer for the misjudgement.

Market surveillance may examine at any time whether the exception applies. Article 6(3) is no free pass. It is a self-assessment you have to document.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 6(3) takes pure support functions out of the high-risk class, but it demands documentation under Article 6(4) and registration under Article 49(2). Profiling always rules it out.

quiz.questionText: An SME uses Personio. Its AI Performance Summaries feature automatically summarises 360-degree feedback before a manager reads it. How should this use be classified?

answerOptions.text: Limited risk because the system only produces a summary
High risk under Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 4(b)
Minimal risk because a human makes the final decision
A prohibited practice under Article 5(1), point (c)

quiz.explanation: Annex III, point 4(b), covers AI used to evaluate performance in employment. AI that decides which parts of the feedback stand out shapes the evaluation. A human deciding at the end does not settle the question once the AI forms the input.

quiz.questionText: Which system is high-risk through Article 6(1) and Annex I rather than Annex III?

answerOptions.text: AI in a lift-control system as a safety component under Directive 2014/33/EU
An applicant-management system that ranks candidates
Credit scoring used by a cooperative bank
AI used by a vocational school to monitor examinations

quiz.explanation: A lift-control system is a standard Annex I case: AI as a safety component of a product covered by EU harmonisation law under Article 6(1). HR ranking falls under Annex III, point 4; credit scoring under Annex III, point 5(b); and examination monitoring under Annex III, point 3. Those three use Article 6(2).

quiz.questionText: What must a provider do when relying on Article 6(3) to classify an Annex III system outside the high-risk category?

answerOptions.text: Nothing needs to be documented
Document the assessment under Article 6(4) and register the system under Article 49(2)
The system is exempt from every AI Act obligation
Profiling is permitted as long as it is preparatory

quiz.explanation: Article 6(3) is not a blanket exemption. The assessment must be documented under Article 6(4), and the system must be registered in the EU database under Article 49(2). Market-surveillance authorities may review the assessment. Profiling prevents reliance on the exception.

lessons.title: Limited risk: transparency under Article 50
lessons.subtitle: Where AI interacts with people or generates content, a disclosure duty applies from 2 August 2026

sections.title: Who is responsible, and from when
sections.content:
How does a customer know she is chatting with a machine? From 2 August 2026 that stops being a question of courtesy and becomes Article 50. The transparency level hits **providers** (paragraphs 1 and 2) and **deployers** (paragraphs 3 and 4). Providers build the system, deployers put it to work in their own house.

Application: from **2 August 2026** (Article 113, point (c)). The rationale sits in Recital 132. People need to know when they are talking to a machine or looking at artificial content. Transparency is the price of the mass market.

Fine for an infringement: **up to EUR 15 million or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover** (Article 99(4), point (g)), whichever figure is higher. One level below Article 5, and still enough to finish off an SME.

Transparency here is no formality. One of the four cases is enough, and a parallel high-risk classification does not lift the duty.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026 and hits providers as well as deployers. Fines run up to EUR 15 million or 3% of annual turnover under Article 99(4), point (g).

sections.title: The four transparency cases
sections.content:
Article 50 counts four cases:

- **Paragraph 1, AI interaction:** providers must design systems for direct interaction with natural persons so that the person recognises she is interacting with an AI system. Exceptions: an obvious AI nature, and, under narrow conditions, law enforcement.
- **Paragraph 2, synthetic content:** providers of generative systems for audio, image, video, or text must mark covered outputs in **machine-readable** form. The solution has to be effective, interoperable, robust, and reliable as far as technically feasible and in line with the state of the art. The Regulation prescribes no single technology.
- **Paragraph 3, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation:** deployers must inform the people affected, where the system is permitted under Article 5 at all.
- **Paragraph 4, deepfakes and AI text on matters of public interest:** deployers must disclose deepfakes visibly, in an adapted form for artistic, creative, satirical, or fictional works. Certain AI-generated text on matters of public interest has to be disclosed unless a natural or legal person carries editorial responsibility.

An ordinary synthetic product photo is not automatically a deepfake. The provider of the generative system can still be caught by the machine-readable marking duty in paragraph 2. For an AI blog article about public affairs with nobody taking editorial responsibility, paragraph 4 can bite.
sections.keyTakeaway: Four cases: the chatbot notice, machine-readable marking of synthetic content, information where emotions or biometrics are read, and visible deepfake disclosure plus AI-text disclosure where no one edits.

sections.title: What limited risk does not mean
sections.content:
Article 50 demands **no** technical high-risk duties. No risk-management system, no technical documentation, no conformity assessment. Only visible or machine-readable disclosure.

But Article 50 **does not fall away** where a system is high-risk at the same time. An HR chatbot that screens applicants sits under two regimes at once: Article 50(1) for the chatbot notice **and** Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 4, for risk management, logging, and human oversight.

Article 50 always hits the specific role holder. For chatbots and synthetic content the **provider**, for emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deepfakes, and AI text the **deployer**. Platforms on which the content appears fall under separate Digital Services Act rules.

A blanket footer notice is not enough. The disclosure belongs where the person meets the content.
sections.keyTakeaway: Limited risk means disclosure, not the technical duties. Article 50 and the high-risk regime run in parallel where both sets of conditions are met.

sections.title: Your rights as an AI user
sections.content:
Article 50 binds providers and deployers. You are the one who benefits.

**From 2 August 2026 the AI interaction has to be recognisable.** Providers of systems built for direct interaction must design them so that the person is informed before or at the first interaction, unless the AI nature is obvious anyway (Article 50(1)).

**Deepfake disclosure and technical marking are two different duties.** Providers of covered generative systems mark outputs in machine-readable form under paragraph 2. Deployers who publish deepfakes disclose the artificial generation or manipulation visibly under paragraph 4, in an adapted form for artistic, creative, satirical, or fictional works.

**Code of Practice on transparency (10 June 2026):** the voluntary code supports the implementation of Article 50(2), (4), and (5). It is a compliance aid, not a substitute for the statutory text, and no automatic proof of conformity.

**What can you actually do?**

1. **Report:** send suspicious or misleading content through the published reporting channel of the platform in question.
2. **Check:** examine origin, context, and the original source. Detection tools give indications, not proof of authenticity.
3. **Check the complaint route:** Article 85 provides for complaints to the competent market-surveillance authority. Germany's KI-MIG entered into force on 29 July 2026 and gives the Federal Network Agency the role of market-surveillance authority, single point of contact, and complaints office, as far as no specialised authority is competent. For the filing itself, use the currently published route.

Technical detection methods for AI-generated content go deeper in the deepfakes module of the learning path.

(Source: Articles 50 and 85 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; European Commission, Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, 10 June 2026; German Bundestag decision on the KI-MIG, 11 June 2026)
sections.keyTakeaway: The role-based duties in Article 50 bite from 2 August 2026. Technical marking and visible disclosure are assessed separately, and for a complaint, check the current route directly with the Federal Network Agency.

quiz.questionText: A print company's marketing team publishes blog articles written independently by an AI system. No person reviews or edits them. Which obligation applies?

answerOptions.text: None, provided the content is accurate
A general footer notice that the company uses AI
Visible disclosure on each article as AI-generated under Article 50(4), second subparagraph
Registration of the AI system in the EU database under Article 49

quiz.explanation: Article 50(4), second subparagraph, requires disclosure for AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest where no person assumes editorial responsibility. A generic footer notice is insufficient; the disclosure must be visible with the content.

quiz.questionText: A construction company uses a chatbot on its careers page. It answers applicants' questions and pre-sorts CVs by experience. Which regime applies?

answerOptions.text: Only Article 50(1), the AI-interaction notice
Only Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 4
Both in parallel: Article 50(1) and Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 4(a)
Neither Article 50 nor Annex III because the system only pre-sorts applications

quiz.explanation: The risk categories are not mutually exclusive. Once a system performs an Annex III function, the high-risk obligations apply in addition to Article 50. The construction company needs the AI-interaction notice as well as risk management, logging, and human oversight.

quiz.questionText: Who is responsible for deepfake disclosure under Article 50(4)?

answerOptions.text: The provider of the AI model, such as OpenAI
The deployer that discloses the deepfake to the public
The platform on which the deepfake appears
The photographer who created the original image

quiz.explanation: Article 50(4) expressly addresses the deployer that uses and discloses the deepfake. Providers have a separate machine-readable marking obligation under paragraph 2. Platforms are subject to the Digital Services Act.

lessons.title: Minimal risk and the decision tree
lessons.subtitle: Most AI in an SME lands here. Six questions decide whether yours does.
keyConcepts: Minimal risk as the residual category

sections.title: What minimal risk means in practice
sections.content:
The biggest risk class in an SME is the one the Regulation never names. **Minimal risk** is the remainder: everything that falls neither under Article 5, nor under Article 6 (Annex I or III), nor under Article 50.

Typical SME examples:

- ChatGPT for internal email drafts
- DeepL for translations with no personal data
- quality-control image recognition on the production line with no personal data
- spam filtering on the mail server
- predictive maintenance on machine data
- route planning, warehouse management
- GitHub Copilot for code completion

Obligations: **no risk-class-specific AI Act duties**. But **Article 4 on AI literacy** applies to every class, the minimal one included. Article 95 encourages voluntary codes of conduct on top.

Minimal risk does not mean: no AI system. Where the tool meets the definition in Article 3(1), a machine-based system with a degree of autonomy that generates outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions, it stays an AI system. Only in the lowest class.
sections.keyTakeaway: Minimal risk is the residual class. No specific duties, but Article 4 on AI literacy has applied since 2 February 2025 regardless.

sections.title: The decision tree: six questions in order
sections.content:
Work through these six questions in order, for each use case rather than each tool.

1. **Is it an AI system under Article 3(1)?** If not, a hard-coded Excel formula for instance, the AI Act does not apply.
2. **Does it fall under Article 5(1), the prohibitions?** If yes, switch it off or rebuild it. Done.
3. **Is it a safety component under Annex I (Article 6(1))?** If yes, high-risk. Sectoral conformity assessment plus Articles 8 to 15.
4. **Does it influence a decision in one of the eight Annex III areas (Article 6(2))?** If yes, high-risk. Articles 8 to 15 plus Articles 26 and 27. Examine the exception in Article 6(3), which has to be documented.
5. **Does it fall under one of the four Article 50 cases?** Chatbot, synthetic content, emotion or biometrics, deepfake or AI text with no editorial responsibility. If yes, limited risk with a transparency duty.
6. **All of them no?** Minimal risk. The duties are Article 4 plus voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95.

The tree runs **per use case**, not per tool. ChatGPT for the meeting summary: minimal. ChatGPT for pre-sorting applications: Annex III, point 4, and therefore high-risk. Same tool, different class.
sections.keyTakeaway: Six questions, in this order, per use case. The same ChatGPT is minimal for emails and high-risk for pre-sorting applicants.

sections.title: The asymmetry of misclassification
sections.content:
Classify wrongly and you either miss the controls you need or pay for controls you do not.

**Too low** (treating high risk as minimal): risk management, logging, or human oversight can be missing. Once the relevant duties apply, market-surveillance measures and the penalty frame in Article 99 come into play. Parallel law such as the General Equal Treatment Act or the GDPR can bite earlier.

**Too high** (treating minimal as high risk): unnecessary compliance work, system by system.

**How to do it:** document the purpose, the role, and the Article 6 assessment against the annexes. Where a legal question stays open, write it down and set a risk-appropriate interim control, instead of a label picked from the gut.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets 2 December 2027 as the application date for stand-alone Annex III systems. Waiting until then would be a mistake.

**Apply it now:** take your most important AI system and work through the six questions. Risk class plus reasoning belong in your AI inventory, in the risk-classification column.
sections.keyTakeaway: A wrong classification costs in both directions. Where doubt remains, document the open legal question and set a risk-appropriate interim control.

quiz.questionText: A tax adviser uses DATEV's AI-assisted receipt capture to identify invoice amounts and assign accounts. What is the risk profile?

answerOptions.text: Prohibited under Article 5 because it involves profiling
High-risk under Annex III, point 5, because it concerns creditworthiness
Minimal risk: it makes no decision about a person and triggers neither Annex III nor Article 50
Limited risk because the account assignment is automated

quiz.explanation: Receipt capture assigns data to accounts. It does not involve a prohibited practice under Article 5, a safety component under Article 6(1), an Annex III area under Article 6(2), or an Article 50 trigger. It therefore falls into the minimal-risk remainder. Article 4 on AI literacy still applies.

quiz.questionText: Which obligation still applies to minimal-risk AI use?

answerOptions.text: Human oversight under Article 14
AI literacy under Article 4
Transparency obligations under Article 50
A fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27

quiz.explanation: Article 4 on AI literacy applies across the risk classes and has done since 2 February 2025 (Article 113, point (a)). Article 14 bites only for high risk, Article 50 only where a transparency case is present, and Article 27 only for the deployers and high-risk cases named there.

quiz.questionText: An IT service provider with 40 employees uses ChatGPT for (a) meeting summaries, (b) email drafts, and (c) pre-selecting freelancer profiles. How should each use be classified?

answerOptions.text: All three are minimal risk because they use the same tool
Uses (a) and (b) are minimal risk; use (c) is high-risk under Annex III, point 4(a)
All three are high-risk because ChatGPT is a general-purpose AI model
All three are limited risk because Article 50 always applies to ChatGPT

quiz.explanation: The decision tree applies to each use case rather than each tool. Meeting summaries and email drafts do not make employment decisions and are minimal risk. Pre-selecting freelancer profiles filters candidates for employment and falls under Annex III, point 4(a). When a general-purpose AI model is used in a high-risk system, the obligations attach according to the concrete use and the relevant role.

props.title: The risk pyramid in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
props.caption: Play the sequence, from the strictest level at the top (prohibited) to the freest at the bottom (minimal). These four levels are exactly what the decision tree checks.

props.title: Order the four risk levels
props.prompt: Sort the risk classes in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 from the deepest regulatory intervention at the top to the lowest at the bottom. Drag the cards or use the arrow buttons.
props.hint: First question: is it prohibited? Then: high-risk? Then: does a transparency duty apply? What is left over is minimal risk.
